facts.title: A Romanian Mine Mystery
facts.text: Tellurium was first detected in 1782 by the Austrian mineralogist Franz-Joseph Muller von Reichenstein while studying a puzzling gold ore from mines near Zlatna in Transylvania (now Romania). The ore behaved so strangely that he nicknamed it 'aurum paradoxum' (paradoxical gold) because it did not act like any known metal. He correctly suspected a new element but could not fully identify it, leaving the puzzle unsolved for years.

facts.title: Named After the Earth
facts.text: The element got its name in 1798 from the German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, who confirmed Muller's discovery and chose the Latin word 'tellus,' meaning earth. This makes tellurium a cosmic counterpart to selenium (from the Greek 'selene,' the Moon) and uranium (named for the planet Uranus). Klaproth made a point of crediting Muller for the original find rather than claiming it himself.

facts.title: The Garlic-Breath Element
facts.text: Tiny amounts of tellurium absorbed by the body produce a powerful, long-lasting garlic-like odor on the breath, sweat, and skin called 'tellurium breath.' It is caused by the body converting tellurium into volatile dimethyl telluride. The effect is so sensitive that exposure to mere micrograms can leave a person reeking for weeks, which is one reason chemists handle it with great care.

facts.title: Rarer Than Gold
facts.text: Tellurium is one of the scarcest stable elements in Earth's crust, with an abundance of only about 1 part per billion, roughly on par with or even rarer than platinum and gold. Despite this, it is not prohibitively expensive because it is recovered as a byproduct of copper refining. Most of the world's tellurium is collected from the anode slimes left behind during electrolytic copper purification.

facts.title: It Came From the Stars
facts.text: One reason tellurium is so rare on Earth is cosmic: studies suggest much of the universe's tellurium is forged in neutron-star mergers and supernovae through rapid neutron capture, the so-called r-process. In 2013, astronomers reported detecting tellurium in extremely old stars, supporting the idea that these violent events seeded the early galaxy with the element. So the tellurium in your electronics genuinely originated in some of the most extreme explosions in the cosmos.

facts.title: Powering Solar Panels
facts.text: The single largest use of tellurium today is in cadmium telluride (CdTe) thin-film solar cells, a leading technology for utility-scale photovoltaics. CdTe absorbs sunlight extremely efficiently, so the active layer can be just a few micrometers thick, far thinner than traditional silicon. This makes tellurium quietly important to the global shift toward renewable energy.

facts.title: The Memory Inside Your Devices
facts.text: Tellurium is a key ingredient in phase-change materials such as germanium-antimony-tellurium (GeSbTe, or GST), used in rewritable CDs, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. The trick is that a quick laser or electrical pulse can flip tellurium-rich alloys between a crystalline and an amorphous state, which reflect light or conduct electricity very differently. The same physics now powers emerging phase-change computer memory chips.

facts.title: A Helper Metalloid in Metals
facts.text: Adding small amounts of tellurium to steel, copper, and lead dramatically improves their machinability, letting factory tools cut them faster and more cleanly. In lead-acid car batteries, tellurium strengthens the lead plates and improves their durability. These metallurgical roles consume a meaningful share of global tellurium even though each part contains only a trace.

facts.title: Not Needed By Life
facts.text: Unlike its chemical cousin selenium, which is an essential nutrient, tellurium has no known biological role in humans and is considered toxic in larger doses. Interestingly, certain bacteria and fungi can resist tellurium compounds and reduce them into metallic deposits, which scientists exploit in microbiology to identify specific microbes. Researchers are also investigating tellurium-based compounds for possible antimicrobial and anticancer activity.

facts.title: A Semiconductor That Reacts to Light and Heat
facts.text: Elemental tellurium is a silvery-white, brittle metalloid that behaves as a semiconductor, and remarkably its electrical conductivity increases when exposed to light. It also combines with elements like bismuth to form bismuth telluride, the most widely used material in thermoelectric devices that convert heat directly into electricity. These coolers and generators run portable refrigerators and even helped power instruments on deep-space probes.
